chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Roy Eldridge in Denver: Joe Pass and his months in Basie's band
summary: Over an all-night talk Roy told stories: his view of guitarist Joe Pass, Basie asking for a pay cut then handing him $200 to bet, and being given no solos so he paid for his own arrangements.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: But a lot of funny things have happened. In fact taped I couple of things, he came to see me when I was at the Cherry Creek Inn here recently, and we talked from the time that I closed around 1:00 o'clock until 8:00 in the morning. And my wife had a little tape recorder, and we didn't know did all these things. This is when the classics come better, when you know you're not on tape and you're talking freely, you know. But Roy did mention one thing. Can I tell about this?

Well anyway, Roy says, "Smack," he says, "now you know we went to Europe, and I always have been a lover of a great guitarist named Joe Pass, and Joe can play. I still say this." And I know the history pretty well on Joe, and they toured Europe with Roy and Jaws on this thing, and had sessions, and Roy mentioned that, "Yeah, he can play, but he ain't going to play it all four beats. When he get ready,
he going to just lay out or going to get in your way, you know, when you're playing, one of those things.

I said, "Joe Pask?" He said, "Yeah, Joe Pask." But Joe plays the solos, one of these things, and that's it. And so I said, "Well, so and so, and I said, Well, okay, we'll leave it like that because I still love Joe Pask." So we got talking about Basie, and a funny thing came up. He said he walked up to Basie one day, and he said, "Basie, what you paying me all this bread for, man?" He said, "And I want to play something." He said, "Why don't you let me play?" Basie said, "What do you want to play?" He said, "Anything." And Basie said, "Like what?" He said, "Like anything, man, just let me play. Don't pay me all this bread, or something."

So this went into a lot of things -- it was a funny thing, and we laughed, and he says, "It's funny now. It wasn't funny then," he says. But he said, one time Basie cried on him. He said -- this was a funny little thing -- he said Basie wanted him to take a $100.00 cut. He was telling him how were bad hard times with band money, and these things, and he said, man, he was about to make him shed tears, he was telling him how bad things were, you know, and you felt sorry for Basie, you know. So he said, "Everything was all right," he said, but about three or four days later he went to the racetrack for Basie, and Basie gave him $200.00 to play on the horses, man. He said, the man wanted me to take a $100.00 cut and give me
Now where is the money coming from? Oh, man, that was the funniest thing. And he'd ask a fellow just fell out. (Unintelligible).

And he talked about the section when he first came into Basie's band. You know, he said that, you know, sometimes, he said, when you're jamming for about a year and your eyes get a little rusty from reading, you know, if you don't -- you know, some of the movements get away from you. He said -- he had an intricate part one time, and he passed it over to the trumpet player, and on this intricate part he did have a solo, see, down further, and he would pass it over to the trumpet player, thinking he was going to get this part back, and he says, no way.

He said -- just lost one. He said, so that kept him from playing. So he said he had some arrangements made and paid for them himself and passed them out, asked Basie if it was all right -- "these are my arrangements," he said, and they feature me, these artists, so and so and so. So he said, Basie play them once, the movement, and he said he was in the band two or three months, he said. No more. So one day he just got evil and he told the guy, "Give me my music. Pass my music in, here, your uniforms, so -- that was a funny thing.
